title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In managed care, distribution is won once a year in the CMS bid and the employer RFP—but unit economics are won or lost every day in claims adjudication, network contracting, and reserve accuracy.
epigraph.author: Actuarial & Operating Economics Review, FY2025–2026

web_blocks.title: Go-to-Market Channels: Brokers, Employer RFPs, and Annual CMS Bidding

web_blocks.html: UnitedHealth Group's customer acquisition engine runs across three distinct sales funnels. In Employer & Individual, national benefits consultants (Mercer, Aon, Willis Towers Watson) and regional brokers run most mid-market and Fortune 500 RFPs. They grade network discount depth, administrative PEPM fees, and specialty-pharmacy integration [1], [2]. Because switching insurers disrupts employee doctor ties and HR payroll feeds, large-employer retention routinely exceeds 95%. In Medicare & Retirement, growth turns on the annual June CMS bid cycle. Actuaries project county medical cost trends 12 to 18 months ahead and factor in CMS's Final Rate Notice (+5.06% net average for CY2026; +2.48% net average for CY2027) [9], [10]. They then set supplemental benefits (dental, vision, Part B givebacks) to attract seniors during the October–December Annual Enrollment Period. Sales flow through captive agents, e-brokers, and the flagship AARP co-branding license. In Community & State, multi-year state Medicaid RFP awards grant regional contracts based on clinical quality, behavioral integration, and local provider adequacy.

web_blocks.title: Claims Float, Pharmacy Supply Chain, and Working-Capital Mechanics

web_blocks.html: Structurally, UnitedHealthcare enjoys negative working capital on its insurance book. CMS and commercial employers remit monthly premiums at the start of each coverage month. By contrast, medical claims take weeks to be incurred, submitted by hospitals, adjudicated, and paid. Measured by Days Claims Payable (DCP)—medical claims payable divided by average daily medical costs—UNH held 44.1 days at Q4 2025. Management rebuilt DCP to 48.6 days at Q1 2026 and held 47.0 days at both Q2 and Q3 2026 [3], [4], [5], [6]. That ~47-day claims float supports a massive investable cash and short-term bond portfolio. That portfolio produced $3,920 million in consolidated investment and other income in FY2025 [18]. However, the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) Medicare Part D redesign altered pharmacy cash-flow timing in 2025. Combined with billions in interest-free provider loans after the 2024 Change Healthcare attack, operating cash flow fell from $29.1 billion in 2023 to $24.2 billion in 2024 and $19.7 billion in FY2025 [14], [18].

On the pharmacy supply chain side, Optum Rx acts as the clearinghouse and buying pool between drugmakers, wholesale distributors, retail pharmacy chains, and plan sponsors. Historically, PBMs earned a mix of administrative fees, retail spread pricing, and retained manufacturer rebates. Facing intense FTC and bipartisan legislative scrutiny in 2025–2026 [13], Optum Rx sped up its shift toward transparent cost-plus and 100% rebate pass-through contracts. This move cuts reliance on opaque spread pricing across commercial accounts. Instead, Optum Rx leans on Optum Specialty Pharmacy dispensing volume, biosimilar adoption (such as Humira biosimilars), and per-claim service fees to defend its ~4.75% operating margin [18], [23].

web_blocks.caption: FY2025 Consolidated P&L and Free Cash Flow Waterfall (Audited Form 10-K, $ Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of $447,567M in FY2025 revenue, $364,650M (81.5%) went directly to medical costs ($313,995M) and cost of products sold ($50,655M), leaving $18,964M in operating earnings (4.24% margin) and $12,807M in net earnings, while generating $19,697M in CFO and $16,075M in Free Cash Flow.

web_blocks.html: The audited FY2025 Form 10-K waterfall reveals the extraordinary operating leverage—and sensitivity—in UnitedHealth Group's unit economics [18]. Direct medical costs ($313,995 million) plus cost of products sold ($50,655 million, largely Optum Rx drug acquisition costs) consumed $364,650 million, or 81.47% of consolidated revenue. Operating costs excluding D&A consumed $59,592 million (13.31% of revenue). Those costs cover clinical payroll, SG&A, broker commissions, and technology, as UNH does not break out staff pay separately on its income statement. Depreciation and amortization added $4,361 million (0.97%), leaving $18,964 million in earnings from operations (4.24% margin). Interest expense took $4,002 million, net losses on subsidiary sales and held-for-sale assets took $265 million, and income taxes took $1,890 million (a 12.9% effective tax rate). Consolidated net earnings stood at $12,807 million (2.86% net margin), with $12,056 million attributable to common shareholders after $751 million of noncontrolling interests [18], [24]. Despite P&L compression, cash conversion stayed resilient. Operating cash flow of $19,697 million minus $3,622 million of capex yielded $16,075 million of free cash flow (125.5% of net earnings) [18].

web_blocks.title: Unit-Economics Sensitivity: Why 100 Basis Points of MCR Moves Billions
paragraphs: On $352.2 billion of FY2025 premium revenue, every 100 basis points (1.0%) of Medical Care Ratio movement equals roughly $3.52 billion of pre-tax operating earnings.
That math explains why Q3 2026's 150-basis-point MCR drop (from 89.9% to 88.4%) drove a 52% YoY jump in quarterly operating earnings to $6.6 billion, even as revenue dipped 0.4%.

web_blocks.title: Medicare Advantage Bid Mechanics & PBM Rebate Economics

web_blocks.html: In Medicare & Retirement ($171.3B FY2025 revenue), pricing discipline follows the annual CMS benchmark-and-bid auction [3], [9]. Each county carries a CMS benchmark rate adjusted by the health plan's Star Rating. Plans at 4.0+ stars earn a 5% quality bonus to their benchmark plus higher rebate retention [15]. Each June, UnitedHealthcare submits an actuarial bid showing its expected cost to deliver standard Part A and Part B benefits for an average-risk senior. When the bid falls below the county benchmark, CMS returns part of the gap as a rebate. The plan must return that rebate to enrollees via lower Part B premiums, $0 drug deductibles, or supplemental dental and vision benefits [9], [10]. If actual medical use exceeds the June bid, the insurer absorbs 100% of the cost overrun until the next calendar year.

In Optum Rx ($151.3B FY2025 revenue), unit economics are shifting from spread and retained-rebate models toward transparent fee structures [18], [23]. Under legacy PBM contracts, Optum Rx negotiated volume rebates from brand-name drugmakers, passing most to clients while keeping a small slice. Amid FTC enforcement and bipartisan PBM bills in 2025–2026 [13], Optum Rx rolled out 100% rebate pass-through and transparent cost-plus pharmacy pricing [23]. It protects its ~$7.2 billion operating profit pool through per-claim admin fees, mail-order dispensing efficiency, and high-margin specialty fulfillment for complex biologics.

book_paragraphs: If you want to know why a single percentage point in UnitedHealth Group's Medical Care Ratio can swing quarterly profits by a billion dollars, you and I need to trace the company's distribution pipes and unit economics down to the penny. Unlike a software firm that sells licenses year-round, UnitedHealthcare wins or loses its year in two rigid annual windows: the fall employer RFP season for commercial benefits, and the June CMS bid deadline for Medicare Advantage.

Think about the discipline—and the trap—of that June CMS bid. Actuaries sit down in May and June of 2025 to price what a 75-year-old senior's hip replacement, outpatient cardiology visit, and Part D specialty drugs will cost in December 2026, eighteen months into the future. They fold in CMS's Final Rate Notice—which granted a +5.06% net average increase for 2026 and a tighter +2.48% net average increase for 2027—and decide how generous to make the zero-dollar dental and vision perks that attract seniors via AARP-branded plans and independent brokers.

Once premiums start flowing in on January 1, the working-capital math becomes a thing of beauty. Employers and CMS wire premiums at the beginning of each month, while hospitals and doctors take weeks to submit and collect on claims. In Q3 2026, UnitedHealthcare held 47.0 Days Claims Payable—meaning it sat on roughly a month and a half of unpaid claims reserves at any given moment. That float funds a massive investment portfolio that generated $3.92 billion of investment and other income in FY2025.

Now look at the audited FY2025 P&L waterfall together, because the scale is staggering. Out of $447,567 million in total revenue, $364,650 million—more than 81 cents of every dollar—went straight out the door for medical costs ($313,995 million) and Optum Rx drug costs ($50,655 million). Another $59,592 million covered operating costs, clinical staff, and SG&A, and $4,361 million went to depreciation and amortization. What remained was $18,964 million in operating earnings—just 4.24 cents on the dollar.

Below the operating line, $4,002 million went to interest on acquisition debt, $265 million went to losses on subsidiary divestitures, and $1,890 million went to income taxes, leaving $12,807 million in consolidated net earnings. Yet even in its worst operational year in a decade, the cash machine kept humming: operating cash flow hit $19,697 million against just $3,622 million in capital expenditures, producing $16,075 million in free cash flow.

That razor-thin 4.2% operating margin is the key to everything you and I watch in 2026. On $352 billion of annual premiums, a 100-basis-point shift in the Medical Care Ratio is worth $3.5 billion of pre-tax profit. When Hemsley and DeVeydt walked away from 1.8 million underpriced lives in 2026 and shaved 150 basis points off Q3's MCR to 88.4%, quarterly operating earnings jumped 52% even while revenue shrank slightly. In managed care, disciplined shrinkage beats undisciplined growth every single time.

To really feel the tension inside UnitedHealth Group's unit economics, put yourself in the shoes of a Medicare Advantage actuary sitting at a desk in Minnetonka every June. CMS gives you a county benchmark—and if your plan earned four stars or better, CMS boosts that benchmark by 5%. Your job is to bid the exact cost of keeping an average senior healthy over the next calendar year. Bid too high, and you lose market share to Humana or Elevance because you cannot afford flashy zero-dollar dental and vision perks. Bid just 1% too low, and on a $171 billion Medicare book, you just vaporized $1.7 billion of operating profit with no way to reprice until next January.

Meanwhile, across the enterprise at Optum Rx, the unit-economics game is evolving from opaque rebates to transparent service fees. Under intense pressure from the FTC and Congress, Optum Rx spent 2025 and 2026 moving clients onto 100% rebate pass-through contracts. Instead of profiting from the spread between what a manufacturer rebates and what an employer sees, Optum Rx increasingly earns its keep on predictable per-prescription administrative fees and the complex cold-chain logistics of Optum Specialty Pharmacy. That shift lowers regulatory tail risk while keeping cash generation remarkably steady.

book_callouts.label: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.title: The 47-Day Float and the 100-Bps Lever
book_callouts.text: UnitedHealth Group is a thin-margin, massive-float business. It keeps roughly four cents of operating profit on every revenue dollar, which means a tiny 1% miscalculation in senior hospital utilization wipes out a quarter of operating earnings—and a 1% pricing fix restores it just as fast.
